analysis.one_liner: Lets banks appeal federal regulators' supervisory decisions to a review panel that includes an industry-recommended judge.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after a House subcommittee hearing in July 2017, it sat in the Financial Services Committee until the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a three-judge panel with the power to overturn federal banking regulators' 'material supervisory determinations' — the formal actions examiners take against a bank. The panel could not defer to the regulator's judgment, and one of its three judges had to be recommended by a bank or a bank trade association. It also set deadlines for regulators to finish exam reports and answer banks' requests for guidance. It was introduced in February 2017, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never advanced past a subcommittee hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and other financial institutions, especially those hit with a supervisory determination such as an enforcement action or a downgrade. They would gain a fast-track appeal before a panel that must judge the matter fresh, with no deference to the agency, plus guaranteed deadlines for exam reports and answers to their legal and accounting questions. The bill would also require regulators to publish summaries of their determinations as industry-wide guidance.

how_it_helps.text: Gives banks exclusive jurisdiction to appeal a final material supervisory determination to a new Independent Examination Review Panel, with a hearing and a decision required within roughly 60 days [S2][S3].
Bars the panel from deferring to the examiner or the agency — it must independently decide whether the regulator's action was appropriate [S3].

Requires one panel judge to be chosen from candidates recommended by a financial institution or a bank trade association, and lets the panel's published decisions serve as precedent for future disputes [S3].

Sets deadlines for regulators: an exit interview within about 9 months of an exam, a final exam report within 60 days of the exit interview, and a written answer to a bank's request for permission or legal interpretation within 120 days [S2][S3].
Prohibits regulators from retaliating against a bank or delaying favorable agency action because the bank appealed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal banking regulators, who would lose final say over their own supervisory decisions and face binding deadlines. More broadly, depositors and taxpayers bear the indirect cost if appeals and delays weaken oversight of shaky banks, since bank failures fall on the deposit insurance fund.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banking regulators, indirectly depositors and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The appeals structure tilts toward the regulated industry: one of the three judges must come from a candidate recommended by a bank or a bank trade association, so the industry helps pick the panel that reviews actions against it [S3].

Requiring the panel to give no deference to the regulator's judgment invites relitigation of examiner calls — the kind of on-the-ground judgments about loan quality and management that agencies argue are best made by supervisors, and delays can let weak banks operate longer [S3].

Publishing summaries of individual determinations as industry guidance could pressure regulators toward predictable, lenient treatment, since every hard call becomes public precedent a bank can appeal against later [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a fair argument on the banks' side: examiners wield heavy powers and banks historically have had few ways to challenge a final supervisory call, and firm deadlines respond to exams that can drag on. But the design leans sharply toward the regulated industry — an industry-recommended judge, a no-deference standard, and publication of determinations as precedent — which would make it harder for regulators to act quickly against problem banks. The public benefit is modest and indirect; the main benefit goes to regulated institutions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, got a subcommittee hearing in July 2017, and never received a committee markup or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Rothfus introduced the bill on February 7, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1][S5].
The Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit held a hearing on the bill on July 12, 2017, before referral — the furthest it advanced [S5].
The full committee never marked up the bill and the House never voted on it; the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banking regulators kept the final word on their supervisory determinations, since the industry-friendly appeals panel was never created. Banks that wanted a formal appeal route gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Keith Rothfus
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it to a subcommittee hearing; no further action resulted.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Republican in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, held one subcommittee hearing, and never brought it to a full committee markup or the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Republican sponsorship — one sponsor and one Republican cosponsor — and no Democratic support is recorded; it died in a committee controlled by the same party.

industries.note: The bill would give banks a fast appeal from regulator actions before a panel partly staffed with an industry-recommended judge and no deference to the agency. Its passage would have made it harder for regulators to enforce actions against problem banks, with risks shifted to depositors and the deposit insurance fund.

industries.industry: Federal banking regulatory agencies (FDIC, OCC, Federal Reserve, NCUA)
industries.note: Regulators would lose exclusive control over their supervisory determinations, face binding deadlines on exams and guidance requests, and see their decisions published as precedent. Their interest in keeping supervision effective runs alongside the public's.

industries.industry: Bank law firms and accounting/consulting practices
industries.note: A formal appeals process, mandatory written determinations, and published precedent would create a steady stream of appeal and advisory work for lawyers and accountants serving banks. The bill requires panel judges to be licensed attorneys and CPAs.
